title: Recalling a patient after an abnormal screening mammogram

header.contentArea: Communicating an abnormal screening result and the assessment process

related.why: The examination that forms part of the assessment clinic this recall leads to
A related scenario of managing anxiety around an uncertain breast finding

brief.scenario: Mrs Beaumont, 56, attended routine NHS breast screening and has been recalled after her mammogram showed an area needing further assessment. She has no symptoms and is understandably anxious.
brief.task: Explain the recall and the assessment process to her. You have 7 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Be clear that recall does not mean cancer is likely, most recalls are not cancer, but that proper assessment is still needed to find out either way.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Either overstating reassurance ("it's definitely nothing") or underplaying it in a way that causes disproportionate alarm before any further tests are done.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I know being called back can feel worrying - can I explain what this recall actually means?"

flow: Acknowledge her anxiety about being recalled
Explain what the mammogram showed in plain terms
Explain what recall does and doesn't mean statistically
Explain the assessment process she'll go through today

grid.label: Acknowledging her anxiety
grid.fail: Moves straight into technical explanation without acknowledging how worrying this can feel.
grid.pass: Explicitly acknowledges that being recalled can feel worrying before explaining further.
grid.high: Validates this without assuming the degree of her anxiety, leaving room for her to describe how she's actually feeling.

grid.label: Explaining the mammogram finding
grid.fail: Uses technical radiological language she is unlikely to understand.
grid.pass: Explains in plain terms that the mammogram showed an area that needs a closer look, without yet saying what it is.
grid.high: Avoids naming a specific worrying-sounding term (e.g. mass, mcircumscribed) until it can be properly explained with context.

grid.label: Explaining recall statistics
grid.fail: States or implies that being recalled means she likely has cancer.
grid.pass: Explains that most people recalled for further assessment do not turn out to have cancer.
grid.high: Gives this context without over-reassuring either, being clear that assessment is still needed to know for certain either way.

grid.label: Explaining the assessment process
grid.fail: Cannot describe what will happen at the assessment clinic.
grid.pass: Explains that she may have further mammogram views, an ultrasound, and possibly a needle biopsy, often all on the same day.
grid.high: Explains roughly when she can expect results, and that a same-day answer isn't always possible if biopsy is needed.

grid.label: Addressing concerns
grid.fail: Dismisses a specific worry she raises without addressing it.
grid.pass: Responds honestly and sensitively to a specific concern she raises.
grid.high: Checks in on how she's feeling about the plan before moving forward, rather than only providing facts.

grid.label: Closing
grid.fail: Ends without confirming she understands what happens next.
grid.pass: Checks her understanding and confirms the next steps in the assessment clinic before proceeding.
grid.high: Offers ongoing support (e.g. a chaperone, a support leaflet, or a contact) through what may be an anxious wait for results.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Your mammogram showed an abnormality, we need to do more tests to see if it's cancer.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There's a mass with irregular margins on the mammogram, so we need further imaging and probably a core biopsy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right, that's everything - the nurse will call you through shortly.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I know being called back can feel worrying - can I explain what this recall actually means?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes, please - I've been really anxious since the letter came.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Your mammogram showed an area that needs a closer look, which is why you've been asked to come in today.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It's worth knowing that most people who are recalled like this do not turn out to have cancer, though we do need to assess it properly to know for sure.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: You may have some extra mammogram pictures, an ultrasound scan, and possibly a small needle sample, often all in the same visit.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Will I get the results today?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Sometimes yes, but if a needle sample is taken, that can take a bit longer to come back - we'll let you know clearly either way before you leave.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Does that make sense so far, and do you have any questions before we start?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I imagine getting that recall letter felt quite frightening - how have you been feeling since?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Honestly, I've barely slept, I've been assuming the worst.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's such a common reaction, and understandable. Your mammogram showed an area that needs a closer look - that's genuinely all we know at this point, nothing more specific than that yet.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I want to say clearly - most people who come back for assessment like this do not turn out to have cancer, but I also don't want to promise you an answer before we've actually looked properly, which is what today is for.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You'll likely have some further mammogram views and an ultrasound, and depending on what those show, possibly a small needle sample from the area - often all done in one visit, though not always.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: I'm terrified of the waiting if I don't get an answer today.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's completely understandable, and I don't want to pretend that wait is easy if it happens - we'll be as clear as possible today about what's been found and when you'll hear back, and there's support available if the wait feels hard.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Does all of that make sense, and is there anything else on your mind before we get started today?

failures.move: Implying recall means cancer is likely.
failures.consequence: Causes disproportionate distress before any actual assessment has taken place, when most recalls are not cancer.

failures.move: Offering blanket reassurance ("probably fine") rather than addressing her specific fear honestly.
failures.consequence: Can feel dismissive and may not actually reduce her anxiety if it doesn't address what she's specifically worried about.

failures.move: Failing to explain that results might not be available the same day.
failures.consequence: Leaves her unprepared for a potentially anxious wait, which could otherwise be softened by clear expectation-setting.

recovery.when: You implied recall meant likely cancer
recovery.line: I should be clearer - most people recalled like this don't turn out to have cancer, though we do need to check properly.
Let me actually address what's specifically worrying you, rather than just saying it's probably fine.

knowledge.fact: The majority of women recalled for further assessment after routine breast screening do not have breast cancer.
Assessment following an abnormal screening mammogram commonly includes further mammographic views, ultrasound, and needle biopsy, often performed in a single visit.
Results are not always available on the same day as assessment, particularly if a needle biopsy sample requires laboratory processing.

recall.think: Recall isn't a diagnosis; assessment is needed.
recall.say: "I can't promise an answer before proper assessment."
do: Acknowledge her anxiety, then explain plainly
Give honest context: most recalls aren't cancer
Set expectations for assessment and any wait

numbers.meaning: typically within a few weeks to the assessment appointment

recall.trap: Implying cancer is likely, or empty reassurance.
recall.finish: Clear explanation, honest statistics, realistic expectations.

partner.opening: Please explain this patient's screening recall and the assessment process to her. You have 7 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mrs Beaumont, 56, recalled after routine screening, with no symptoms yourself. You've been very anxious and have barely slept since receiving the recall letter, assuming the worst.

reveals.finding: You admit to barely sleeping and assuming the worst.

reveals.trigger: Candidate explains recall statistics honestly, without over-promising
reveals.finding: You feel somewhat reassured but still anxious about the wait.

reveals.trigger: Candidate addresses your fear of not getting same-day results
reveals.finding: You feel more prepared for the possibility of waiting.

push.question: Does being recalled mean I probably have cancer?
push.expect: Explain that most recalls are not cancer, while being honest that assessment is needed to know for certain.

push.question: Will I definitely know today?
push.expect: Explain that results are sometimes available same-day, but not always, particularly if biopsy is needed.

curveballs.prompt: My mother died of breast cancer, so this feels especially frightening for me.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledge this personal context with genuine care, without letting it change the honest clinical information given, and offer additional support given her personal history.

curveballs.prompt: Can you just tell me now if you think it's cancer or not?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Be honest that this cannot be judged from the mammogram alone before proper assessment, avoiding both false reassurance and speculative alarm.
